newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia Moslem scholars urge heavy voter turnout.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia Moslem scholars urge heavy voter turnout.

text.p: Indonesia's influential Council of Ulemas (MUI) on Monday urged Moslems to vote in large numbers in the May 29 general elections, saying it would help the country's development.

"The MUI urges Moslems, as good citizens, to be morally responsible by using their rights to vote for the continuation of national development under the New Order," it said in a statement faxed to Reuters.

The statement came amid controversy over whether it was against the law for Indonesians not to vote in the general elections. President Suharto has said the authorities would take action against people who encouraged others not to vote.

The unrecognised left-wing People's Democratic Party (PRD) said in a statement on Monday that it had renewed its call asking people to boycott the elections, which it said had been engineered by the government.

The PRD, which has gone underground after most of its leaders were arrested on subversion charges in the wake of riots in Jakarta last July, has been behind a recent poll boycott graffiti campaign which has drawn the authorities ire.

"We ask (pro-democracy supporters) to boycott the general elections in 1997. In addition to delegitimising this undemocratic election, this boycott also aims to serve as a platform which unites people who are pro-democracy," the statement said.
The subversion trials of PRD members are continuing. Subversion carries a maximum penalty of death.

Earlier this month, authorities arrested former legislator Sri Bintang Pamungkas and two other leaders of his unrecognised United Indonesian Democratic Party of Indonesia (PUDI) on subversion charges for advocating a poll boycott.

The ulema council said it wished to stress the importance of the election, which it said implemented the people's sovereignty. The statement gave no further details and chairman Hasan Basri was not available for comment.

The MUI groups Indonesian Moslem religious scholars and the government often seeks advice from the council in matters related to Islam. About 90 percent of Indonesia's 200 million people are Moslems, making it the world's most populous Moslem nation.
The New Order is the term used to describe President Suharto's government after he rose to power in the 1960s following an abortive coup blamed on the banned Indonesia Communist Party (PKI).
Authorities in West Java are searching for people who produced some 6,000 pamphlets calling for a boycott.

The ruling Golkar party, the Moslem-based United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) are the only three political parties allowed to contest the elections.
